title: The exile (2 Kings 25)
hook: Jerusalem falls in 587 BC and the Temple burns

segments.voice: Yesterday, Naaman, a proud general told to wash seven times in the Jordan. Your line was go and wash. What simple thing did you finally do? Day four hundred fourteen, and a new week.

Last week we stood inside Solomon's Temple as a cloud filled it. Today we watch it burn. The books of Kings have been warning about this for chapters: king after king turning away, prophet after prophet calling them back. Now the army of Babylon surrounds Jerusalem, under King Nebuchadnezzar, Nabuchodonosor in the Douay-Rheims. The siege drags on from the ninth year of the king into the eleventh. The food runs out. The text says it in one line: there was no bread for the people of the land. Then the walls are breached, in 587 BC by one common reckoning, and the last king of Judah runs for it in the night.
screen: `THE TEMPLE THAT WAS FILLED WITH CLOUD.` → `BABYLON SURROUNDS JERUSALEM.` → `NO BREAD IN THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Today's word is exile, and 2 Kings tells it with almost no comment, which makes it worse. King Zedekiah, Sedecias in the Douay, is caught near Jericho. His sons are killed in front of him, and then his eyes are put out, so that this is the last thing he sees. The next month the Babylonian commander arrives, and the Douay says simply: "he burnt the house of the Lord, and the king's house, and the houses of Jerusalem." The walls are pulled down. The people are marched off to Babylon, far to the east. Only the poorest are left behind to tend the vines and fields. Exile means more than moving. It means losing the land God promised, the king from David's line, and the Temple where God chose to dwell, all at once. Some scholars think much of the Hebrew Bible took its final shape in its shadow. This path has been here before. Back on day one hundred eighty-nine we sat with the psalm of the exiles, Psalm one thirty-six in the Douay: "Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept: when we remembered Sion." And the question they asked: "How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?" Today we've seen why they were weeping. But listen to how 2 Kings ends. Not with the fire. Decades later, a new king of Babylon lets David's descendant, Jehoiachin, out of prison, speaks kindly to him, and gives him a seat at his table for the rest of his life. A small, strange thread of hope. The line of David isn't finished.
screen: `THE LAST KING OF JUDAH, BLINDED.` · `THE HOUSE OF THE LORD BURNS.` · `UPON THE RIVERS OF BABYLON.` · `A SEAT AT THE KING'S TABLE.` · then, large: `HOW SHALL WE SING IN A STRANGE LAND?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for people who've lost their home. Settle, and breathe. Think of people who are, right now, far from the place they belong. Refugees crossing borders. Families whose houses burned or flooded. Someone sleeping in a car. Maybe someone in your own life who had to leave everything. Picture them sitting by strange waters, remembering home. If you pray, you can hold them before God, and ask for whatever they most need. If you don't, simply let yourself feel their loss for a moment, without looking away. The bell holds the time.
Exile. Being forced from your homeland; for Judah, the fall of Jerusalem, the burning of the Temple, and the long years in Babylon. Today's word.
Your line: by the waters again. Today, do one concrete thing for someone far from home: a donation, a welcome, a call to a friend who moved. Day four hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the fall of Jerusalem in the Mass readings, pray Psalm 137 (136 in the Douay) on the Fourth Sunday of Lent in one year of the cycle, and the Church remembers the Holy Family's flight into Egypt when it speaks of care for migrants and refugees.

original.note: Hebrew: exile, captivity. In later Jewish thought, galut also names the long condition of living away from the land.

trapdoor: what you thought: the people of Judah moved to Babylon.
what it means: in one stroke they lost the land, the king from David's line, and the Temple. a deep wound, and the end of 2 Kings still leaves a thread of hope.
what a scholar hears: some scholars think much of the Hebrew Bible took its final shape in and after the exile; the date is 587 or 586 BC depending on how the reigns are counted.

notes: Date: the outline says 587 BC; many scholars prefer 586. The script says 'in the summer of 587 BC by the usual reckoning' and the trapdoor gives both. Confirm.
Siege length: from the ninth year, tenth month to the eleventh year, fourth month of Zedekiah (25:1–3), about eighteen months; 'about a year and a half'. Confirm.
Refers back to Catholic path day 189 (By the rivers of Babylon); confirm the day number stays correct.
'Much of the Bible was shaped in its shadow' / 'many scholars think' is a common scholarly view; stated cautiously.

Psalm 137 is the responsorial psalm for the Fourth Sunday of Lent, Year B (with 2 Chronicles 36); confirm. Pius XII's Exsul Familia (1952) on the Holy Family as refugees is the background to howItsDone.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'a week ago' corrected (day 408 was six days earlier); the siege length and 'a month later' now follow the regnal dates in 25:1–8; 'hundreds of miles', 'the deepest wound in the Old Testament' and 'the usual reckoning' cut; the psalm is no longer said to be written by the exiles; myth item reworded off a dating claim.
